687.title: The hungry ghosts
687.hook: in Chinese communities, the seventh month's offerings to hungry ghosts and lost souls
687.howItsDone: In Chinese communities during the seventh lunar month, families make offerings of food, incense and paper goods, temples hold rites to feed hungry ghosts, and some communities stage performances with front-row seats left empty for unseen guests.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Obon, welcome fires and the circle dance, and your line, they come home. Whose story did you tell? Today, a new week, and the guests nobody invites. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

Singapore, the seventh month of the lunar calendar. On the sidewalks, small fires burn in metal bins, paper offerings curling into ash. Little piles of oranges, rice and incense sit along the curbs. In open-air tents, singers perform loud, cheerful shows, and the front row of seats is left empty. Nobody sits there. Those seats, people say, are for the guests you can't see. Yesterday, Moggallana's mother was one hungry ghost, and her son could help her. In Chinese communities, this whole month is for all the others: the ghosts nobody remembers. Today: the hungry ghosts.
screen: `THE SEVENTH LUNAR MONTH.` → `OFFERINGS ON THE CURB.` → `THE EMPTY FRONT ROW.`

segments.voice: In Buddhist teaching, hungry ghosts, peta in Pali, preta in Sanskrit, are one of the realms of rebirth. Beings driven by craving so strong that nothing satisfies it. East Asian art pictures them with huge, empty bellies and throats as thin as a needle: always hungry, never able to swallow enough. The image is a teaching in itself. Craving, made visible. The Pali canon already speaks of them. A short text, the discourse outside the walls, pictures dead relatives standing outside houses, at crossroads and by doorposts, returning to their old homes, waiting. When the living give food and drink, and dedicate the merit to them, the ghosts rejoice. In China, these threads came together with older customs of honoring the dead. On the fifteenth night of the seventh month, Buddhist temples hold the Ullambana rites you heard about yesterday; Taoists keep the same night as the Zhongyuan festival. Often the two are woven together, and families may not draw a sharp line. In some temples, monks perform a ritual of feeding the hungry ghosts, scattering food and chanting so that it can reach beings who can't otherwise eat. Notice who the month is really for. Not your own grandparents only. The lost ones. Those who died far from home, or with no one left to remember them. The festival is a kind of public kindness toward strangers who can't say thank you.
screen: `PETA: ALWAYS HUNGRY.` · `HUGE BELLY, NEEDLE THROAT.` · `WAITING OUTSIDE THE WALLS.` · then, large: `FEED THE HUNGRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer food to someone hungry. Sit, and settle. First, notice hunger in yourself, any kind: for food, for attention, for something to be different. Don't judge it. Just see it, like the ghost's thin throat. Then widen out. Think of the hungry people near you, a shelter, a person on a corner, a neighbor stretched thin. Choose one way to feed someone today: a meal bought, a food bank gift, a plate shared. The bell holds the time.
The hungry ghosts. Peta, beings whose craving can never be satisfied, fed with offerings in the seventh lunar month in Chinese communities. Today's word.
Your line: feed the hungry. Today, feed someone who can't thank you, or give to a place that feeds strangers. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

688.title: Pavarana
688.hook: at the rains' end monks invite each other to point out their faults
688.howItsDone: At the end of the rains retreat, Theravada monks gather and each in turn formally invites the community to point out his faults; lay communities in Thailand, Laos and Myanmar mark the same full moon with merit-making and festivals of light.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the hungry ghosts and the empty front row, and your line, feed the hungry. Who did you feed? Today, three months after the rains began, they end, with a strange invitation. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

Imagine your workplace holds a meeting at the end of the year. Everyone sits in a circle, and one by one, starting with the most senior person, each one says to the group: if you've seen me do anything wrong, or heard of it, or even suspected it, please tell me. Out of kindness, tell me. Most offices would rather do anything else. Buddhist monks have done exactly this at the end of every rains retreat for over two thousand years. It's called Pavarana, the invitation. Today: Pavarana.
screen: `A CIRCLE AT YEAR'S END.` → `IF YOU SAW ANYTHING, TELL ME.` → `THE INVITATION.`

segments.voice: The Vinaya tells how it began. A group of monks spent a rains retreat together and, to avoid any quarrel, agreed not to speak to each other at all, all season. They got through it peacefully, and went to tell the Buddha. He did not praise them. Living together like that, in silence to avoid friction, isn't living at ease, he said. Instead, he set a practice. At the end of the rains, each monk invites the community to speak to him about anything seen, heard or suspected. Out of compassion, speak to me, the invitation goes, and if I see the fault, I will make amends. Three times each monk says it. Notice what the three are. Seen, heard, suspected. Not just proven. You're inviting the uncomfortable thing someone wasn't sure enough to say. The Connected Sayings tell how the Buddha himself did it. At one Pavarana, sitting with five hundred monks, he invited them first: is there anything I have done, in body or in speech, that you would criticize? Sariputta answered for them: no, sir. The teacher went first. In Thailand, Laos and Myanmar, this full moon also brings festivals of light: candles and lanterns, boats of light on rivers, and in some places the story that the Buddha came down from heaven this very day, which we'll meet in two days. But the core is a sentence. Tell me my faults. It's a hard sentence, and a brave one, and it keeps a community honest.
screen: `SILENCE TO AVOID QUARRELS.` · `THE BUDDHA DIDN'T PRAISE IT.` · `SEEN, HEARD, SUSPECTED.` · then, large: `TELL ME MY FAULTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: invite one piece of honest feedback. Sit, and settle. Bring to mind someone who knows you well and wishes you well. A friend, a partner, a colleague. Notice what happens in the body as you imagine asking: is there anything I do that you think I should see? Tightness? Heat? Let it be there, and breathe with it. Then picture their answer arriving, and you taking it in, calmly, with thanks. The bell holds the time.
Pavarana. The invitation at the end of the rains, when each monk asks the community to point out any fault seen, heard or suspected. Today's word.
Your line: tell me my faults. Today, ask one person you trust for one honest piece of feedback, and simply say thank you. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

689.title: Kathina, deeper
689.hook: cloth offered, a robe cut and sewn by the community within a day
689.howItsDone: In Theravada communities, lay people bring Kathina cloth and other gifts to a monastery in the month after the rains; the monks formally give the cloth to one of their number, and in Myanmar some temples hold overnight robe-weaving contests.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pavarana, and your line, tell me my faults. Did you ask for one honest word? Today, the season after the rains, and a robe that has to be finished by dawn. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

You met Kathina in your first year: the thirty monks who arrived at the end of the rains in muddy robes, and the Buddha's allowance of new cloth. Today we go inside the ceremony itself. It's late in the evening at a monastery in Myanmar. In a hall lit with bulbs, teams of young women sit at wooden looms, racing. They've been weaving since the night before. By dawn, the robes must be woven, finished and offered. Crowds come to cheer them on. It's a contest, and also something older: a gift that must be made in a single stretch of time. Today: Kathina.
screen: `THE MUDDY ROBES, REMEMBERED.` → `LOOMS RACING THROUGH THE NIGHT.` → `DONE BY DAWN.`

segments.voice: Kathina has a few rules that make it unlike any other gift. First, timing. It can be held only in the month after the rains retreat ends, and only at a monastery where monks have completed the retreat. Second, the cloth must be offered freely. Monks can't ask for it, hint at it, or arrange it. Lay people bring it, unasked, to the whole community, not to one monk. Third, the community decides. In a formal act, the monks agree together to give the cloth to one of their number, often someone whose robes are worn or who is respected for his conduct. Then the fourth rule, the one in today's line: the robe must be made that very day. The old texts describe cloth washed, measured, cut, sewn, dyed and finished before dawn, with the whole community helping. In some places today the cloth arrives already made, and the community completes the formal act the same day. And the Myanmar weaving contest, held on an autumn full moon, carries the old urgency in a new form. Why a single day? The texts don't explain. Some teachers point to what it does: it gathers everyone at once, lay and monastic, around one task. No one person can do it alone. The robe that comes out is ordinary cloth. What's special is the night everyone spent making it together.
screen: `ONLY AFTER THE RAINS.` · `CLOTH GIVEN UNASKED.` · `THE COMMUNITY CHOOSES ONE.` · then, large: `SEWN IN A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mend or sew something. If you have a needle and thread nearby, and something with a loose button or small tear, you can do it after the bell. For now, sit, and picture it. The cloth in your hands. The needle going in and out, slowly, each stitch a breath. Notice how mending asks for patience: you can't rush a stitch. If sewing isn't for you, think of one small thing in your home that needs repair, and picture fixing it, carefully, today. The bell holds the time.
Kathina. The cloth offering after the rains: given unasked, given to one monk by the community's choice, and made into a robe in a single day. Today's word.
Your line: sewn in a day. Today, mend one thing, a button, a sock, a squeaky hinge, and finish it before you sleep. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

690.title: Lhabab Duchen
690.hook: in Tibet, the day the Buddha descended after teaching his mother in heaven
690.howItsDone: On Lhabab Duchen, Tibetan Buddhists visit temples, make offerings, recite prayers and mantras, circle stupas and give generously; in Thailand the descent is remembered at the end of the rains with a large alms-giving ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kathina, the looms through the night, and your line, sewn in a day. What did you mend? Today, a story told across the Buddhist world, about a son and his mother. Day six hundred ninety.

The Buddha's mother, Maya, died seven days after he was born. He never knew her. The tradition tells a story about that loss. Many years later, after his awakening, the Buddha rose to a heaven where his mother had been reborn as a god, and spent a whole rains retreat there teaching her. Then he came back down. In Tibet, the day he came down is one of four great holy days of the year. Today: Lhabab Duchen.
screen: `MAYA DIED SEVEN DAYS AFTER.` → `HE NEVER KNEW HER.` → `HE WENT UP TO TEACH HER.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the commentaries and later texts, and with many variations. In the Theravada telling, the Buddha spent the rains in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, where his mother, reborn among the gods, came to hear him, and he taught the higher teaching, the Abhidhamma. Each day, the story goes, he passed a summary to Sariputta on earth, which is one way the tradition explains how the Abhidhamma reached us. When the rains ended, he descended at a place called Sankassa, on a staircase that the gods made: by tradition a jeweled stair in the middle, with gold and silver stairs on either side, the gods Brahma and Sakka attending him. Crowds waited at the bottom. In Tibetan, Lhabab Duchen means 'the great occasion of the descent from the realm of the gods.' It falls on the twenty-second day of the ninth Tibetan month, usually in November. People visit temples, make offerings, recite, circle stupas and holy places, and give generously. In Thailand, the same descent is remembered at the end of the rains, with a great alms round where monks walk down a hill or steps, like the Buddha coming down to the waiting crowd. Notice the shape of the story. He went up to give his mother the best thing he had. And then he came down, back to the people waiting. He didn't stay in heaven.
screen: `A RAINS RETREAT IN HEAVEN.` · `TEACHING HIS MOTHER.` · `A STAIRCASE AT SANKASSA.` · then, large: `HE CAME DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor your mother. Sit, and settle. Bring to mind your mother, or whoever mothered you: a grandmother, an aunt, a foster parent, a teacher, a friend. If that relationship is painful or absent, you can choose someone else who cared for you, or simply wish well to all mothers. Picture giving them the best thing you have to give: time, a word of thanks, a kindness. Then picture coming back down to your ordinary day, carrying that warmth with you. The bell holds the time.
Lhabab Duchen. The Tibetan holy day of the Buddha's descent, after a rains retreat spent teaching his mother in heaven. Today's word.
Your line: he came down. Today, call, write or think of your mother, or someone who mothered you, and give them something good. Day six hundred ninety.

the higher teaching, passed each day in summary to Sariputta, the story goes.

691.title: Bodhi Day
691.hook: December 8 in Japan: the awakening; Zen monasteries sit for a week
691.howItsDone: In Japanese Zen monasteries, Rohatsu sesshin is a week of intensive sitting in early December, often ending with an all-night sit; many Buddhist communities in the West mark Bodhi Day on December 8 with meditation and readings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lhabab Duchen, the stair at Sankassa, and your line, he came down. Did you give your mother, or someone who mothered you, something good? Today, winter in Japan, and the night of the awakening. Day six hundred ninety-one.

Early December in a Zen monastery in Japan. It's cold. The meditation hall is often unheated. For the past week, the monks have been sitting from before dawn until late at night, with short breaks for meals, work and a little sleep. On the last night, in many monasteries, nobody lies down at all. They sit through until morning. Then, just before sunrise, someone looks up at the eastern sky, where one bright point is still shining. Today: Rohatsu.
screen: `DECEMBER IN A ZEN MONASTERY.` → `A WEEK OF SITTING.` → `THE LAST NIGHT, NO SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Rohatsu means 'the eighth day of the twelfth month.' In Japan, that's when the Buddha's awakening is remembered, and since Japan moved to the solar calendar, temples there keep it on December eighth. Other East Asian communities mark it on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, and in China it's a day for a sweet porridge, laba congee, recalling the milk-rice the Buddha was given before his awakening. Theravada lands keep the awakening together with the birth and the passing, on Vesak. Different calendars, the same night under the tree. The Pali texts tell the night in three watches. In the first, the Buddha recalled his past lives. In the second, he saw how beings pass away and are reborn according to their deeds. In the last watch, he understood suffering, its cause, its end and the way, and his mind was freed. And as the night ended, dawn came. Later tellings, especially in East Asia, add one detail that has become central in Zen: he looked up, saw the morning star, the planet Venus, low in the eastern sky, and awoke. In Zen, that moment is retold again and again: a star he had seen many times, seen now completely. The Rohatsu retreat follows the same shape: a week, building to a last night without sleep, ending at dawn. It retells the story with the body. The monks aren't waiting for a star. They're practicing being awake when it rises.
screen: `THE EIGHTH DAY, TWELFTH MONTH.` · `THREE WATCHES OF THE NIGHT.` · `A STAR AT DAWN.` · then, large: `THE MORNING STAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit late tonight. Not all night. Just a little later than usual, after the house is quiet. For now, sit, and settle. Picture the cold hall, the rows of cushions, the long last night. Feel the stillness of it. Then picture the sky just before dawn, dark blue, one bright point low in the east. Let your attention be as clear as that point. When you sit tonight, a few minutes is enough. And if you're up before sunrise sometime this week, look east. The bell holds the time.
Rohatsu. The eighth day of the twelfth month, when Japanese Buddhists remember the awakening, and Zen monasteries sit through a week that ends at dawn. Today's word.
Your line: the morning star. Tonight, sit a few minutes later than usual, and if you're up early, look east for the brightest point. Day six hundred ninety-one.

692.title: Nirvana Day
692.hook: February 15 in East Asia: the Buddha's passing remembered
692.howItsDone: In Japan and many Mahayana communities, temples mark Nirvana Day (Nehan-e) around February 15 by hanging a painting of the Buddha's passing, chanting, and reading from the account of his last days; Theravada Buddhists remember the passing on Vesak.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rohatsu, the night of awakening, and your line, the morning star. Did you catch a star, or the first light, before the day got loud? Today, the other end of the same life. Day six hundred ninety-two.

In a temple in Japan in mid-February, a huge painted scroll is unrolled and hung. In the middle, a man lies on his right side between trees, head resting on his hand. Around him, crowds are weeping: monks, kings, gods. And animals. An elephant on its back. A tiger. Birds, a snake, a crowd of creatures. It's called a nehan-zu, a picture of nirvana. And it isn't a picture of awakening. It's a picture of a death. Today is Nirvana Day.
screen: `A SCROLL UNROLLED IN FEBRUARY.` → `THE ANIMALS WEEPING.` → `A PICTURE OF A DEATH.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Buddhists use the word nirvana for two things. One is the awakening itself, the fire of craving going out, which we kept yesterday. The other is what happens when an awakened one dies: the final nirvana, parinirvana in Sanskrit, parinibbana in Pali. Nothing is left to be reborn. Nirvana Day remembers that second one. In Japan it's usually kept on February 15; other Mahayana communities keep it then too, or on February 8, or by the lunar calendar. In Theravada lands, as we heard on Vesak, the passing is kept on the same full moon as the birth and the awakening. Same event, different calendars, and nobody is wrong about it. Now the story, from the Book of the Great Decease. The Buddha is eighty. He's ill. He walks to Kusinara, a small town, and lies down between two sal trees. The text says the trees burst into flower out of season and dropped blossoms on him. His cousin Ananda goes off and weeps against a doorpost. The Buddha calls him back, and reminds him: hadn't he always taught that everything dear must change and part? Then he asks the monks three times if anyone has a last doubt. Nobody speaks. And then come his last words. In Rhys Davids's translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Notice what he does with his own death. He doesn't hide it. He uses it as the final lesson. Things put together come apart, including a Buddha. So keep going, carefully. On Nirvana Day, temples chant, read the story, sit. Some temples make little dumplings or rice cakes. The point isn't grief. It's looking straight at an ending, with company.
screen: `TWO MEANINGS OF NIRVANA.` · `A PASSING ON TWO CALENDARS.` · `BETWEEN THE SAL TREES.` · `THE LAST WORDS AS A LESSON.` · then, large: `ALL THINGS END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reflect on one ending. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then let one ending come to mind. Not the hardest one you know. Maybe a school, a house, a friendship that drifted, a pet, a season of life. Look at it the way the scroll looks at the Buddha: plainly, with company around. What was it? What did it give you? If grief comes, let it sit with you too. Ananda wept. At the end, come back to this breath, which is also ending, and the next one, which is beginning. The bell holds the time.
Nirvana Day. February 15 in East Asian Buddhism, remembering the Buddha's final passing, his parinirvana between the sal trees. Today's word.
Your line: all things end. Today, when something small finishes, a meal, a song, a conversation, notice it end, and let it go without rushing to the next thing. Day six hundred ninety-two.

693.title: Losar
693.hook: the Tibetan new year: cleaning the house, new prayer flags, fresh starts
693.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist families prepare for Losar by cleaning their homes, then hang new prayer flags, visit monasteries and shrines, make offerings and visit relatives over the first days of the new year.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nirvana Day, the Buddha's passing between the sal trees, and your line, all things end. Did you notice something small end, and let it? Today, a beginning, and the end of a week. Day six hundred ninety-three.

A week of festivals, looked at together. The hungry ghosts fed. Monks inviting each other to name their faults. A robe sewn in a single day. The Buddha coming down from heaven. The morning star. The passing between the sal trees. Yesterday ended with an ending. So today the calendar turns over. In Tibetan homes, a few days before the new year, everybody grabs a broom. Corners get scrubbed. Old dust goes out the door. Today is Losar.
screen: `A WEEK OF FESTIVALS.` → `AN ENDING, THEN A TURN.` → `EVERYBODY GRABS A BROOM.`

segments.voice: Losar is two Tibetan words: lo, year, and sar, new. New year. It follows the Tibetan lunar calendar, so it moves, usually landing in February or early March. It's kept in Tibet and by Tibetans everywhere, and in Bhutan, Ladakh and the Himalayan communities of Nepal, sometimes on different dates. First comes the cleaning. In the last days of the old year, houses are cleaned top to bottom. On the twenty-ninth evening, many families eat a soup called guthuk, with dough balls hiding little objects inside. Find salt and you're said to be lazy; find chili and you're said to have a sharp tongue. Everyone laughs. Then leftover soup and a dough figure are carried out of the house, with the old year's troubles, and left at a crossroads. Next, the flags. Strings of prayer flags, blue, white, red, green and yellow, are printed with prayers and mantras. Over a year, wind and sun fade them to rags. At Losar many families take down the old ones and hang new ones on rooftops and passes. The idea, in Tibetan custom, is that the wind carries the blessings printed on them out to every being it touches. Then the visits. Monasteries hold special rituals and masked dances. Families visit shrines, make offerings, and greet each other with tashi delek, good fortune. Many historians think parts of Losar are older than Buddhism in Tibet, from earlier seasonal festivals. Buddhist practice and those older customs grew up together. Here's what links it to the week. Yesterday: all things end. Losar takes that seriously, and then picks up a broom. The old year is really over. So you clear it out, and begin.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clean one corner. Not the whole house. Just one corner, one drawer, one shelf. Before you start, sit for a moment. Look at the corner. What's piled there from a year that's already gone? Then do it slowly, as practice. Lift each thing. Wipe the dust. Keep what's useful, let go of what isn't. If you'd rather, sit now, picture the corner, and do it later today. Either way, notice the feeling of space when it's done. The bell holds the time.
Losar. The Tibetan new year: lo, year, sar, new. Cleaned houses, new prayer flags, and tashi delek. Today's word.
Your line: a fresh year. Today, after you clean your corner, stand in it for a breath and let something old be over. Day six hundred ninety-three.
